title: The impact of light and colour on psychological mood: a cross-cultural study of indoor work environments
research_question: To determine whether indoor lighting and colour would have any systematic impact on the mood of people working indoors.

participants.description: 468 females and 520 males, aged 18 to 65 years (mean 39.4 SD 9.85 years), working in indoor environments (offices, schools, industrial premises) in four countries: Argentina (27° S), Saudi Arabia (26° N), Sweden (56° N), and the UK (52° N).
participants.recruitment: Employees working at least three-quarters of full time during daytime, excluding night-shift workers and those with previous records of prolonged illness.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Real work environments (offices, schools, industrial premises) in four countries (Argentina, Saudi Arabia, Sweden, UK) with varying latitudes and seasonal day lengths. Environmental features studied included objective illuminance, subjective lightness, subjective interior colour, and physical distance to the nearest window.

measures.instrument: Emotional status index (composite of 12 four-grade rating scales: rested/tired, alert/drowsy, awake/sleepy, interested/bored, efficient/inefficient, devoted/indifferent, secure/anxious, friendly/angry, happy/sad, confident/hesitating, independent/dependent, strong/weak). Coefficient alpha = 0.82.

Four-graded scale (1=clearly insufficient, much too dark; 2=slightly insufficient, a little bit too dark; 3=just right; 4=very bright and glaring, too much light). Between seasons consistency coefficient alpha = 0.82.

Four-graded scale (1=no colour at all, very subdued and monotonous; 2=colours are rather neutral; 3=some colour but not very vivid; 4=very colourful and vivid). Between seasons consistency coefficient alpha = 0.86.

measures.instrument: Horizontal illuminance values (lux) measured with calibrated luxmeters on the desktop.
Computed from sunrise to sunset for each region at five times of the year.

mechanisms: Seasonal variations in day length influence psychological mood, particularly in countries far from the equator.
Subjective perception of lighting (e.g., 'just right' vs. 'too dark' or 'too bright') impacts mood, rather than objective illuminance levels.
Access to windows, especially close proximity, and the presence of colourful interior decoration contribute to a more positive mood.
implementation_implications: Consider seasonal impact and access/distance to windows in design.
Supplement physical lighting measurements with qualitative assessments from occupants.
Implement good colour design to contribute to positive mood, especially in otherwise subdued environments.
Treat light and colour as part of a complex system for a healthy building.

limitations: The study did not detail the specific semantic differences in translated scales across countries, which might affect absolute figure comparisons.
Objective lighting measurements were limited to horizontal illuminance values and did not include various measures of luminance, which might be important for mood.
The study did not directly measure the view function of windows, only distance, which is different from daylight delivery function.
The study did not investigate the impact of tinted glass or shading devices on mood.

The study did not explore the specific characteristics of 'good colour design' or the optimal saturation levels for real environments, noting that very strong colours in laboratory studies sometimes had undesirable results.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper investigates how variations in light exposure due to latitude and season, as well as specific indoor lighting and color, influence psychological mood, often implicitly linking to circadian rhythm disruption.
